title: Nominal clauses and possession

objectives.can: Read a clause with no verb, finding its subject and predicate, and the Hebrew ways of saying 'have'.

explanation.summary: A Hebrew clause does not need a verb. Two nouns, a noun and an adjective, or a noun and a prepositional phrase can simply be set side by side, and the reader supplies 'is', 'was' or 'will be' from the context. The same pattern is how Hebrew says 'have': there is no verb for it.

sections.heading: A clause with no verb
body: In a nominal clause (also called a verbless clause) there are two parts. The subject is what the clause is about. The predicate says something about it: who or what it is, what it is like, or where it is. A predicate may be a noun, an adjective, a participle, a pronoun or a prepositional phrase.

There is no word for the present tense of 'to be' in such a clause. The time comes from the context. The same clause may be read 'is', 'was' or 'will be', depending on where it stands in the story. Do not add a tense that the Hebrew does not show.

sections.heading: The order of the two parts
body: The commonest order is subject first and predicate second, as in the first verse of Psalm 23. But a predicate is often placed first. The tendency is that a predicate placed first is the part that is new or stressed: it answers a question or draws attention. It is a tendency, not a rule, and grammarians differ about how best to explain it, so read each clause on its own terms. Genesis 42:9 puts 'spies' before 'you', and Jonah 1:9 puts 'Hebrew' before 'I'.

A third person pronoun sometimes comes between or after the two parts and ties them together: the verse Exodus 3:5 ends with הוּא. Many grammarians call this use a 'pronoun of connection', and it can be left untranslated or rendered 'it is'.

sections.heading: Existence: יֵשׁ and אֵין
body: Two small words say that something exists or does not. יֵשׁ means 'there is', 'there exists'. Its negative is אֵין, 'there is not'. They are particles, not verbs, and they do not change for tense, gender or number.
אֵין takes suffixes that name the thing that is absent: אֵינֶנּוּ means 'he is not' or 'it is not', 'he is no more'. This is how a speaker says that the boy is gone in Genesis 37:30.

sections.heading: Saying 'have'
body: Hebrew has no verb for 'to have'. The usual way to say that someone has something is to put the owner after the preposition ל, and the thing owned after it as the subject: 'to Laban (are) two daughters' is 'Laban had two daughters'. This is a nominal clause: the ל phrase is the predicate, and the thing owned is the subject.

יֵשׁ and אֵין often join in: יֶשׁ לָנוּ אָב means 'we have a father', and a form of אֵין negates it: 'Hannah had no children'. In narrative, when the time must be stated plainly, a verb from the root הָיָה may be added, as in 1 Samuel 1:2, 'there were children to Peninnah'.
The same preposition ל can mean 'belonging to'. Psalm 24:1 says that the earth belongs to the LORD with the phrase לַיהוָה הָאָרֶץ, with the owner first.

sections.heading: Other ways to show that a thing belongs to someone
body: Inside a phrase, belonging is shown by the construct state ('the name of the man') and by a pronominal suffix on a noun ('his wife'). Those are the relations you learned in the earlier lessons on the construct and the suffixes. The ל construction is for statements of ownership or possession in a clause.

misunderstandings: A Hebrew clause with no verb is not incomplete. It is a normal sentence, and nothing is missing from it.
הוּא in a nominal clause is not always 'he'. Between a subject and a predicate it often just ties them together.
Possession with ל names the owner after the preposition. 'To Laban' is Laban the owner; the thing owned is the subject of the clause, not the object of a verb.
אֵין and יֵשׁ are not verbs. They have no tense or person of their own, and the time comes from the context.

deeper.heading: Why a verb is sometimes added
body: When a writer wants to fix the time of a nominal clause as past or future, or to make it the next step in a story, a form of the verb הָיָה, 'to be', is added. In Genesis 1:2 the earth 'was' formless, with the verb. The nominal clause itself is the default way to describe a state of affairs, and a verb marks something more specific.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: יְהוָה is the subject and רֹעִי is the predicate: 'the LORD (is) my shepherd'. There is no verb, and the subject comes first. The suffix -ִי on the predicate is 'my'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Possession with ל and no verb. 'To Laban (were) two daughters' is 'Laban had two daughters'. The name clauses that follow are nominal too: שֵׁם הַגְּדֹלָה לֵאָה, 'the name of the elder (was) Leah', with a construct chain as the subject and a name as the predicate.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And he had two wives: the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah; and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three ways in one verse. וְלוֹ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים is ל with a suffix and no verb: 'he had two wives'. וַיְהִי לִפְנִנָּה יְלָדִים adds a form of הָיָה, 'there were children to Peninnah'. וּלְחַנָּה אֵין יְלָדִים uses אֵין: 'to Hannah (there are) no children'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And we said unto my lord: We have a father, an old man, and a child of his old age, a little one; and his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loveth him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: יֶשׁ־ is 'there is' and לָנוּ is ל with the suffix 'us'. Together: 'we have a father, an old man'. The thing owned, אָב, follows, with its adjective זָקֵן.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And He said: 'Draw not nigh hither; put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The subject is הַמָּקוֹם, 'the place', with a long relative clause. The predicate אַדְמַת קֹדֶשׁ, 'holy ground' (a construct chain), comes before the pronoun הוּא, which ties it back to the subject. There is no verb 'to be'.

practice.prompt: Which sentence describes the structure of יְהוָה רֹעִי (words 2 and 3)?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A prepositional phrase
A verb followed by its object
A clause with no verb: the subject יְהוָה and the predicate רֹעִי
A construct chain, 'the shepherd of the LORD'
practice.explain: The two words are simply set side by side. יְהוָה is the subject and רֹעִי, 'my shepherd', is what is said about it. The time (here 'is') comes from the context.

practice.prompt: How does this verse say that Laban had two daughters?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: With the object marker אֵת before 'Laban'
With the verb 'to have'
With a verb of giving
With ל and the owner, then the thing owned: 'to Laban (were) two daughters'
practice.explain: Hebrew has no verb 'to have'. The owner follows ל, and the thing owned is the subject. The same pattern stands in every verse with ל of possession.

practice.prompt: What does אֵינֶנּוּ (word 5) say of the child?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he returned unto his brethren, and said: 'The child is not; and as for me, whither shall I go?'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: He is not (there)
He is with us
He will not come
He is not good
practice.explain: אֵין takes the suffix -ֶנּוּ, 'him', and the clause means 'the child is not (there)'. Jacob's son is missing. The verb is not needed.

practice.prompt: What does יֵשׁ (word 5) say in 'יֵשׁ יְהוָה בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה'?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said: 'Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'The LORD is not in this place'
'The LORD was sent'
'There is' (the LORD is) in this place
'The LORD will give'
practice.explain: יֵשׁ is the particle of existence, 'there is'. Jacob says that the LORD is present in this place. The prepositional phrase gives the place.

practice.prompt: In 'seven years they (are)', which words are the subject and which the predicate?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: The seven good kine are seven years; and the seven good ears are seven years: the dream is one.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The subject is הֵנָּה, the predicate is 'seven years'
The subject is 'the seven good cows', the predicate is 'seven years', and הֵנָּה ties them together
There is no subject; the clause is a command
The subject is 'seven years' and the predicate is הֵנָּה, 'here'
practice.explain: The verse interprets the dream: the seven good cows are seven years. The plural pronoun הֵנָּה (feminine, like 'cows') repeats the subject and joins it to the predicate.

check.prompt: What does the final הוּא (word 16) do?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And He said: 'Draw not nigh hither; put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It repeats the subject הַמָּקוֹם and ties it to the predicate 'holy ground'
It starts a new clause: 'he said'
It is the verb 'to be'
It is the object marker
check.explain: In a nominal clause a third person pronoun often connects the subject and predicate. Here it points back to 'the place'; it can be translated 'is' or left out.

check.prompt: What time does וּשְׁמוֹ לָבָן (words 2 and 3) have?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Rebekah had a brother, and his name was Laban; and Laban ran out unto the man, unto the fountain.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a command
It is future, 'his name will be Laban'
It is always present
The clause has no verb, so the context decides; in this story it is past, 'his name was Laban'
check.explain: A nominal clause shows no tense. The verses around it are narrative, so the clause is read as past. The first half of the verse, וּלְרִבְקָה אָח, uses ל of possession: Rebekah had a brother.

check.prompt: Which word is the predicate in לַיהוָה הָאָרֶץ?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: A Psalm of David. The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: לַיהוָה, 'to the LORD', meaning 'belongs to the LORD'
Neither; the clause has no predicate
Both words are subjects
הָאָרֶץ, 'the earth'
check.explain: The subject is הָאָרֶץ and the predicate is the ל phrase, which says whose it is. The predicate is placed first, which puts weight on the owner.

check.prompt: What does אַיִן (word 19) say about the man?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: No shrub of the field was yet in the earth, and no herb of the field had yet sprung up; for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The man was not good
There was no man to work the ground
A man was working the ground
The man would not come
check.explain: אַיִן is the particle 'there is not', here after וְאָדָם. It denies existence; the infinitive phrase tells what the man was lacking for.

check.prompt: What is the ending of אֵינֶנּוּ (word 17)?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And they said: 'We thy servants are twelve brethren, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan; and, behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is not.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'he is not (there)'
A plural noun ending
A 1st person plural suffix: 'we are not'
A verb ending
check.explain: The suffix is -ֶנּוּ with the sense 'him': the one brother 'is not (there)'. The speakers are telling Joseph that one of the twelve is gone.

check.prompt: What time does the clause וּלְשָׂרָה בֵן (words 8 and 9) have?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Is any thing too hard for the LORD. At the set time I will return unto thee, when the season cometh round, and Sarah shall have a son.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A command
Future: Sarah will have a son, as the context shows
Past: Sarah had a son
Present: Sarah has a son
check.explain: There is no verb. The first half of the verse, 'I will return to you', speaks of a future time, and the context makes the clause future. The pattern ל + owner + thing owned is the usual way to express having.

check.prompt: What does וּלְחַנָּה אֵין יְלָדִים say (words 12 to 14)?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And he had two wives: the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah; and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Hannah has children
Hannah is the mother of Peninnah
Hannah gave children
Hannah has no children: ל of possession with the negative אֵין
check.explain: 'To Hannah (there are) no children.' The same pattern with the positive יֵשׁ would say that someone has children.

check.prompt: What does the order עִבְרִי אָנֹכִי (words 2 and 3) do?

quoted.title: Jonah
quoted.english: And he said unto them: 'I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who hath made the sea and the dry land.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Makes אָנֹכִי an object
Changes the clause into a question
Turns it into the past tense
Puts the predicate first, which often gives it stress: 'a Hebrew I am'
check.explain: The clause has no verb: the pronoun is the subject and 'Hebrew' the predicate. A predicate placed first is often the part stressed or new. It is a tendency; both orders occur.

check.prompt: What does יֶשׁ לָנוּ אָב זָקֵן say?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And we said unto my lord: We have a father, an old man, and a child of his old age, a little one; and his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loveth him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: We gave a father
We do not have a father
We have a father, an old man
Our father is old and gave us
check.explain: יֶשׁ is 'there is' and לָנוּ is ל with 'us'. The thing owned, אָב זָקֵן, follows. The pattern is the usual 'have'.

reading.why: The story of Laban's daughters begins with a nominal clause of possession, וּלְלָבָן שְׁתֵּי בָנוֹת, and then uses name clauses with no verb. Such clauses stand beside narrative verbs, so you can see where each kind is used.

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Laban said unto Jacob: 'Because thou art my brother, shouldest thou therefore serve me for nought? tell me, what shall thy wages be?'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: Now Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Leah's eyes were weak; but Rachel was of beautiful form and fair to look upon.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Jacob loved Rachel; and he said: 'I will serve thee seven years for Rachel thy younger daughter.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Laban said: 'It is better that I give her to thee, than that I should give her to another man; abide with me.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.
